title: The Seed Too Small to See
hookLine: a father has his son break a banyan seed until nothing is left to see; Vaisheshika asks where the breaking stops
tomorrow: a sage kicks Vishnu in the chest. what does Vishnu do?

cards: A young man named Shvetaketu has come home after twelve years of study, rather pleased with himself. His father, Uddalaka, isn't impressed yet. Bring me a fruit from that banyan tree, he says.
Here it is. Break it. What do you see?
Tiny seeds. Break one of those. What do you see now?
Nothing at all, sir. And his father says: that fine thing you can't see, my son, out of that, this whole great banyan stands.

teach.h: TAT TVAM ASI: THAT, YOU ARE.
teach.b: That's the Chandogya Upanishad, and Uddalaka goes on: that finest essence is the self of the whole world. That is the real. That is the self.
And that, Shvetaketu, is you: tat tvam asi. Centuries later, another Hindu school asked the same question, where does the breaking stop, and gave a different answer.

teach.h: PARAMANU: THE SMALLEST OF THE SMALL.
teach.b: Vaisheshika said the dividing stops at the paramanu, often translated atom: the smallest of the small. It has no parts, so it can't come apart, and the school calls it eternal, never made and never destroyed.
You can't see one. So why believe it?

teach.h: A MOUNTAIN AND A MUSTARD SEED.
teach.b: Its thinkers argued: if you could divide forever, a mountain would have endless parts, and so would a mustard seed. Then what makes the mountain bigger? So the dividing must stop, at something partless.
In the classic account, atoms pair up, the pairs gather, and you reach the smallest thing an eye can see: a speck of dust floating in a sunbeam. From there, up to clay and rivers and banyan trees.
Atoms of earth, water, fire and air. So two answers, from one tradition. The Upanishad finds one unseen essence, and says it's you.
Vaisheshika finds countless partless atoms, and many selves, which it names later this week. Hinduism keeps both on its shelf, and this path ranks neither.
What they share is the teaching: what you see stands on what you can't, and the unseen doesn't break. A cup breaks; a body ages.

teach.h: THE BREAKING IS IN THE JOINTS.
teach.b: For Vaisheshika, the breaking happens in the joints, not at the bottom of things.

how: Students of Vaisheshika learn the teaching on atoms through the Vaisheshika Sutra and its commentaries, usually alongside Nyaya, as part of traditional Sanskrit study.

he saw nothing at all, and Uddalaka said the whole banyan stands from that unseen fineness.

it argued the dividing stops, or a mountain and a mustard seed would both have endless parts.

games.q: a kid asks you: can you cut something in half forever? by Vaisheshika, what do you say?
o: yes, forever: there's always a smaller half.
no: you reach something partless that can't be cut, the paramanu.
no: it turns into nothing at all.
games.why: Vaisheshika says the dividing stops at the paramanu, a partless thing. otherwise a mountain and a mustard seed would both have endless parts.

practice: Hold a seed, a grain of rice, or just look at your own hand. Imagine breaking it in half, and again, down past what any eye can see.

Then let one thing that has come apart lately come to mind, a plan, a routine, maybe something more, without fixing it, and notice that what it was made of, the care, the time, hasn't simply vanished.
If you pray, rest in what you trust doesn't come apart. If you don't, rest in the breath.

wordCard.voice: Vaisheshika. The school of particulars and of the paramanu: the partless smallest thing, where all dividing has to stop.

orig.note: Sanskrit: paramanu, the smallest particle, often translated atom.

carryVoice: Your line: paramanu, where all dividing stops. The unseen holds up the banyan. Back tomorrow, same hill.
